def: A knee ligament that prevents the tibia from sliding backward on the femur. Injured by a blow to the front of the flexed knee, causing a positive posterior drawer test.
Inflammation of the cecum in neutropenic patients, usually after chemotherapy, causing right lower quadrant pain and fever. Also called neutropenic enterocolitis.
Inflammation and necrosis of the cecum and nearby bowel in patients with severe neutropenia, usually after chemotherapy. Causes fever and right lower abdominal pain.
A procedure that fuses the two pleural layers, usually with talc or other irritants, to prevent recurrent pneumothorax or pleural effusion.
The small kappa or lambda chains of an antibody. Excess free monoclonal light chains appear as Bence Jones protein in multiple myeloma and AL amyloidosis.
A process in which epithelial cells lose their cell-to-cell adhesion and become migratory mesenchymal cells. Important in embryonic development and in cancer invasion and metastasis.
Proteins that speed up Ras's GTP hydrolysis, turning Ras off. NF1 encodes neurofibromin, a Ras GAP, so its loss leaves Ras active.
An enzyme that, bound to cyclin D, phosphorylates Rb to push cells from G1 into S phase. Targeted by palbociclib in breast cancer.
Enzymes that detect and fix damaged DNA, such as mismatch repair and excision repair enzymes. Defects cause cancer predisposition syndromes like xeroderma pigmentosum.
Caspases (such as 8 and 9) that start the apoptosis cascade and cleave downstream executioner caspases.
A cyclin that pairs with CDK2 to drive the G1 to S transition of the cell cycle.
A cyclin that pairs with CDK4 and CDK6 to phosphorylate Rb and drive progression through G1. Overexpressed in mantle cell lymphoma.
A DNA polymerase sliding clamp that holds the enzyme on DNA during replication. Used as a marker of cell proliferation.
RB1, a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13 whose protein Rb restrains the cell cycle at G1/S. Loss causes retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma.
A permanent state of cell-cycle arrest after many divisions or stress, such as telomere shortening. A barrier to cancer.
Signals such as VEGF and FGF that stimulate new blood vessel growth, used by tumors to gain blood supply.
New tumor-specific antigens created by mutations, which can be recognized by T cells.
A death receptor (CD95) on cells; binding of Fas ligand activates caspase 8 and extrinsic apoptosis. Defective in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.
Overuse tendinopathy of the wrist flexor and pronator tendons at the medial elbow, causing pain with gripping.
Finely ground smokeless tobacco used orally or nasally, linked to oral cancers.
The most commonly fractured carpal bone, in the anatomical snuffbox. Fractures risk avascular necrosis of the proximal part because of retrograde blood supply.
A carpal bone that dislocates volarly after hyperextension of the wrist, can compress the median nerve and may develop avascular necrosis (Kienbock disease).
A small sesamoid carpal bone on the ulnar side of the wrist where flexor carpi ulnaris attaches, next to Guyon canal.
The nerve network from L1-L4 that gives off the femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves.
The way a sequence of nucleotides is divided into codons. Insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three cause frameshift mutations.
Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor such as clopidogrel, given after acute coronary syndrome or stent placement to prevent thrombosis.
Showering of cholesterol crystals from atherosclerotic plaque after vascular procedures, causing blue toes, livedo reticularis, kidney injury and eosinophilia.
Signaling lipids made from arachidonic acid, including prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes.
The receptor for IL-6, a cytokine that induces fever and acute phase proteins; blocked by tocilizumab.
Antibodies like evolocumab that block PCSK9, preventing LDL receptor degradation and lowering LDL cholesterol.
A systemic vasculitis causing recurrent painful oral and genital ulcers and uveitis. Associated with HLA-B51 and pathergy.
Restoring blood flow to ischemic heart muscle after a blockage, as with PCI or thrombolytics. Can cause reperfusion injury and arrhythmias.
A protein of muscle caveolae membrane invaginations. Mutations cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and long QT syndrome.
Muscles on each side of the spine, such as erector spinae, that extend and stabilize the back.
Paired skull bones forming the roof and sides of the cranium, joined at the sagittal suture.
A protein made by osteoblasts that binds calcium and marks bone formation. Vitamin K-dependent.
Enzyme that makes large amounts of nitric oxide in macrophages during inflammation to kill microbes.
Changes in size, shape and function of the ventricle after infarction or pressure overload, often progressing to heart failure.
G protein-coupled receptors on cells that mediate prostaglandin effects such as vasodilation and pain.
Infection with Entamoeba histolytica, causing bloody diarrhea and liver abscess.
Mixtures of small peptides from protein digestion, used in culture media.
A thermally dimorphic fungus from Latin America that causes paracoccidioidomycosis, with budding yeast in a "captain's wheel" shape.
An engineered receptor on T cells joining an antibody-derived binding domain to T-cell signaling domains, targeting tumor antigens such as CD19.
A B cell surface marker present on nearly all B cells, targeted by CAR T-cell therapy for B-cell leukemia and lymphoma.
Treatment in which a patient's T cells are engineered to carry a chimeric antigen receptor and reinfused to attack cancer. Risks include cytokine release syndrome.
Mutation caused when DNA, such as a viral vector, inserts into a gene. A risk of retroviral gene therapy.
The process of inducing genetic mutations.
Skin infection with Candida, often in warm, moist skin folds, as red plaques with satellite lesions.
A mass of branching fungal hyphae.
Meningitis from Cryptococcus neoformans in immunocompromised patients, especially AIDS. Diagnosed by India ink or antigen in CSF.
A genus of Mucorales fungi that cause mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis or immunocompromise.
Sac-like fungal structures that contain asexual spores, seen in Mucorales.
Iron-binding molecules secreted by microbes to steal iron from the host.
Hair-like protein appendages on bacteria used for attachment and conjugation.
A regulator protein that inhibits the alternative complement pathway on host cells. Mutations cause atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Uptake of naked DNA from the environment by a bacterium.
The complete DNA of a bacterium, usually a circular chromosome plus plasmids.
A bacterium from bird exposure that causes psittacosis, an atypical pneumonia.
Constriction of the pupils in response to light, via the optic nerve and oculomotor nerve.
Infection by corkscrew-shaped bacteria such as Treponema, Borrelia and Leptospira.
A retroviral gene encoding the capsid and matrix core proteins, including p24.
A flu- or mononucleosis-like illness 2-4 weeks after HIV infection, with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy.
An HIV gene encoding a transactivator protein that boosts viral transcription.
Abnormal fat redistribution, with central fat accumulation and facial and limb fat loss, from HIV therapy.
Clusters of sensory neuron cell bodies, such as dorsal root ganglia.
An enzyme that degrades DNA. Nebulized recombinant form thins sputum in cystic fibrosis.
Replacement pancreatic enzymes (lipase, protease, amylase) taken with meals in pancreatic insufficiency.
A viral skin disease that gave Jenner his smallpox vaccine.
A poxvirus used in early smallpox vaccination.
The poxvirus used as smallpox vaccine.
A prokinetic drug withdrawn for causing long QT and torsades.
An enzyme that reduces nitrate to nitrite, used in bacterial identification.
An enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid, helping bacteria spread.
A hemolytic toxin from group A Streptococcus. Streptolysin O is the basis of the ASO titer.
A viridans group streptococcus in mouth flora that can cause endocarditis.
Stimulation of macrophages (e.g., by interferon gamma) to kill microbes.
Multinucleated cells with nuclei in a horseshoe arrangement, in granulomas of TB.
A mass-like granuloma of TB, often in brain.
TB infection of the lungs.
Tuberculoid leprosy with few bacteria and strong Th1 response.
A skin test antigen for leprosy type.
Lepromatous leprosy with many bacteria and weak cell-mediated response.
Lab technique separating proteins by charge then identifying with antibodies.
A progestin used to stimulate appetite in cachexia and treat endometrial cancer.
Disease of multiple spinal nerve roots.
High-throughput DNA sequencing of many fragments in parallel.
Bacilli that stain purple, including Bacillus, Clostridium, Listeria and Corynebacterium.
Skin wound on the leg, from venous insufficiency, arterial disease or neuropathy.
Carbapenem antibiotic paired with cilastatin, which blocks renal dehydropeptidase.
Age-related breakdown of intervertebral discs.
Hives triggered by sunlight exposure.
Antibody preparation that neutralizes diphtheria toxin.
Bleeding into the eye's vitreous causing floaters, seen in diabetic retinopathy.
Viral retinitis from herpes viruses causing peripheral retinal necrosis.
Eye exam that views the iridocorneal angle with a special lens to classify glaucoma.
A lincosamide antibiotic related to clindamycin.
Drugs activating GABA receptors, like benzodiazepines.
Strain producing botulinum toxin A, used cosmetically.
Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lining airways.
Toxin of Bordetella pertussis raising cAMP.
Polysaccharide layer that resists phagocytosis.
Intracellular bacteria transmitted by ticks causing anaplasmosis.
Inflammation of the ileum, as in Crohn disease.
A paramyxovirus causing respiratory infections in children.
DNA virus family that includes hepatitis B virus.
Rapid, severe liver failure with encephalopathy and coagulopathy.
Mosquito genus that transmits West Nile and St. Louis encephalitis viruses.
An HIV protease inhibitor that causes indirect hyperbilirubinemia.
An HIV protease inhibitor.
An HIV protease inhibitor given with ritonavir.
A chemokine receptor used as a coreceptor by HIV, blocked by maraviroc.
A chemokine receptor used by HIV as a coreceptor.
A fluoroquinolone antibiotic.
A fluoroquinolone antibiotic for urinary infection.
A bacterial enzyme that separates replicated chromosomes, inhibited by fluoroquinolones.
Spread of cancer across peritoneal surfaces.
Bony shelves in the nasal cavity that warm and humidify air.
Gi-coupled receptors blocked by antipsychotics.
A pyrimidine nucleotide used in RNA synthesis.
Parkinsonism caused by drugs, strokes or toxins rather than Parkinson disease.
Drugs that block DNA polymerase, like acyclovir.
Loss of ovarian function before age 40.
Physical breaks in chromosomes, increased in Fanconi anemia and ataxia telangiectasia.
Drugs like irinotecan and etoposide that block DNA unwinding.
The mitotic stage when sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles.
Persistent difficulty discarding possessions.
The first sterol intermediate in cholesterol synthesis, formed from squalene. In fungi it is demethylated by an enzyme that azole antifungals inhibit.
Inflammation of the vulva and vagina.
Antifungal drug class including ketoconazole.
A polysaccharide in fungal cell walls.
Free-living amoeba causing keratitis in contact lens wearers.
Dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias from Trypanosoma cruzi.
Leishmania infection destroying nose and mouth tissue.
A malaria species that forms dormant liver hypnozoites.
Inherited degeneration of the retina, such as retinitis pigmentosa.
Transient pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia, often from migrating helminth larvae.
River blindness from Onchocerca volvulus transmitted by black flies.
Simulium fly that transmits Onchocerca volvulus.
Massive lymphedema with thickened skin, classically from filariasis.
Infection with Wuchereria bancrofti causing lymphedema and elephantiasis.
Infection with Loa loa transmitted by deerflies, causing eye worm and Calabar swellings.
Tapeworm infection, such as Taenia and Diphyllobothrium.
Infection with Schistosoma blood flukes from freshwater snails.
A blood fluke causing hepatosplenic disease.
Chronic painful swelling and draining sinuses from fungal or actinomycete infection.
Enteric fever like typhoid from Salmonella paratyphi.
Cause of paratyphoid fever.
Severe falciparum malaria with coma and seizures.
Ultrasound of the heart during exercise or dobutamine to detect ischemia.
A collection of serous fluid under skin after surgery.
Test measuring acid reflux in the esophagus.
Quitting tobacco use.
Surgery cutting the internal anal sphincter to treat chronic anal fissure.
Tear in the carotid wall causing stroke and Horner syndrome.
Gram-negative species with many serotypes causing gastroenteritis and typhoid.
Small-vessel vasculitis causing palpable purpura, triggered by drugs.
Phospholipids missing one fatty acid, signaling molecules.
Antimalarial combination used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria.
An antimalarial combined with artemether.
An artemisinin antimalarial.
A non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor for HIV.
Undetectable hepatitis C RNA 12 weeks after treatment, equaling cure.
Putting together new viral particles in a host cell.
Type III hyperlipoproteinemia from apoE2 homozygosity, with palmar xanthomas and elevated chylomicron and VLDL remnants.
Exchange of DNA between homologous chromosomes in meiosis I.
Infection with Legionella, as Legionnaires disease.
Fold of tissue connecting tongue to the floor of the mouth.
Bacterial infections transmitted from animals to humans.
Lab test for HLA typing using antibody and complement.
Fluids with lower osmolarity than plasma, causing cells to swell.
Disorders of bone, muscle and joints.
Picornavirus infection causing hand-foot-mouth disease and myocarditis.
Viral red eye with subconjunctival bleeding.
Family of RNA viruses including norovirus.
Mosquito-borne alphavirus encephalitis.
Severe mosquito-borne alphavirus encephalitis.
Alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes causing fever and severe joint pain.
Mosquito-borne alphavirus encephalitis of horses and humans.
Mosquito-borne alphavirus encephalitis.
Family of segmented double-stranded RNA viruses including rotavirus.
Influenza surface protein that binds sialic acid for cell entry.
Vitamin B2 lack causing cheilosis and glossitis.
Loss of cerebral cortex thickness.
Filovirus hemorrhagic fever.
Filovirus causing severe hemorrhagic fever.
Family of segmented negative-strand RNA viruses including hantavirus.
Phlebovirus fever spread by sandflies.
Tick-borne bunyavirus hemorrhagic fever.
